Research summary

Prediction quality is only meaningful when evaluation respects the information available at deployment.

LeakageBench studies a practical model-governance failure: a model can look excellent offline while relying on features, transformations, split logic, or records that would not be valid at the actual scoring moment. The benchmark therefore treats prediction-time information availability as an explicit deployment contract rather than an informal modeling assumption.

The analysis combines an observed dataset condition with controlled integrity tests, compares chronological and random evaluation designs, and reconciles released metric effects independently before a final release decision is exposed to downstream publication artifacts.

Dataset
UCI Bank Marketing ? 41,188 rows ? 20 input fields
Decision moment
Immediately before the current outbound call begins
Evaluation
Chronological 70/15/15 split with random-split comparator
Models

Executive Decision

MEASURED DERIVED
Decision context

The release decision separates a model's offline score from whether the candidate can exist at the production scoring boundary.

Project 7 defines the decision moment before the current outbound call begins. Under that contract, the duration-based candidate and the corrected prediction-time-safe pipeline answer different questions: one tests a known violation, while the other represents the configuration eligible for deployment.

This distinction matters because a blocked leakage scenario should not be misread as evidence that every corrected model must also be rejected. The release gate is attached to the complete candidate configuration: feature contract, evaluation design, transformations, overlap checks, reconciled metrics, and claim provenance.

Method in brief

Unit of decision: model + feature set + evaluation configuration.

Gate sequence: availability ? split integrity ? transformation integrity ? duplicate check ? metric reconciliation.

Public result: corrected Pipeline C passes; the violating duration candidate remains blocked.

Should this model configuration go live?

The release decision depends on what the model can know immediately before the outbound call, not only on its offline score.

The observed duration condition is blocked.

The current-call duration scenario returns BLOCK, while the corrected prediction-time-safe Pipeline C passes the release gate.

Evidence to retain
  • Current-call duration is not available at the pre-call prediction moment.
  • The corrected prediction-time-safe release and the blocked leakage scenario are distinct candidate configurations.
  • Sixty released metric effects reconcile independently with zero mismatches.

Block the violating candidate. Release the safe pipeline.

This separates the integrity decision from the final corrected release status rather than treating them as contradictory results.

Interpretation

The important result is not simply that one ROC-AUC value becomes smaller. The stronger conclusion is that evaluation must be bound to the production information set. A metric obtained from an impossible information state cannot justify release, regardless of how attractive the number appears.

Operational significance

This converts leakage detection from an analyst's post-hoc review into a release-control mechanism. A data or model team can expose one machine-readable decision while retaining the evidence needed to explain why a candidate was passed, warned, or blocked.

Scope & limitation
This decision is specific to the defined pre-call prediction moment and the frozen UCI Bank Marketing benchmark. It is not evidence that the same feature contract applies unchanged to another deployment.

Leakage Cases

OBSERVED DATASET CONDITION CONTROLLED INJECTION
Threat model

Leakage is treated as a family of information-boundary failures, not as one suspicious feature that can be deleted after the fact.

The benchmark deliberately separates three evidence types. The current-call duration case is an observed condition in the source dataset. Random temporal mixing is an evaluation-design experiment. The remaining cases introduce controlled violations so that the auditor's blocking behavior can be tested against known ground truth.

This taxonomy prevents an important reporting error: a controlled injection should not be described as though it were naturally observed in production, while an observed source-data condition should not be dismissed merely because another model happens to show a small metric delta.

Benchmark logic

Five scenarios exercise feature timing, temporal mixing, supervised transformations, duplicate overlap, and post-outcome information.

Auditor behavior and measured metric effect are recorded separately.

Controlled injections validate detection behavior rather than estimate real-world prevalence.

How can evaluation accidentally see information deployment will not have?

Five distinct integrity failures were evaluated.

The benchmark separates an observed dataset condition, an evaluation-design experiment, and controlled injections instead of presenting them as the same kind of evidence.

Evidence to retain
  • S1 captures an observed current-call duration condition.
  • S2 isolates the effect of random temporal mixing relative to chronological evaluation.
  • S4 independently verifies 618 duplicate train/test overlaps in the controlled overlap case.

Gate the integrity mechanism, not only the metric delta.

A small or zero measured performance effect does not make a known leakage mechanism deployment-safe.

Interpretation

Leakage should be diagnosed by mechanism first and metric effect second. A transformation fitted with forbidden target information, for example, is an integrity violation even if a particular benchmark run produces only a modest change in aggregate accuracy.

Why this matters for model governance

A release gate built around mechanisms is more durable than a list of known bad columns. It continues to protect the scoring process when leakage enters through evaluation design, preprocessing, duplicated records, or post-outcome proxies.

Feature Contract

MEASURED PREDICTION-TIME CONTRACT
Information contract

Every model input is evaluated against one explicit prediction moment before model performance is considered.

The prediction-time contract asks a simple but frequently omitted question: would this exact value exist, in this form, when the production system requests a score? Features known before the call can be eligible; values produced during or after the call cannot. Unknown semantics are blocked rather than guessed.

The treatment of campaign illustrates the conservative policy. The source metadata does not establish the exact counter semantics needed to prove what the value represents immediately before the current call. The benchmark therefore records the uncertainty and prevents the field from silently entering the release candidate.

Contract classes

PRE_DECISION and KNOWN_AT_DECISION can be eligible.

DURING_ACTION and POST_OUTCOME are blocked.

UNKNOWN remains blocked until its production semantics are documented.

Which inputs actually exist at scoring time?

Duration is unavailable; campaign remains unresolved.

Duration is classified as DURING_ACTION. Campaign is blocked because the source metadata does not establish exact production counter semantics immediately before the current call.

Evidence to retain
  • The prediction moment is immediately before the current outbound call begins.
  • Duration is classified DURING_ACTION and is therefore blocked.
  • Campaign remains UNKNOWN because exact production counter semantics are not established by the source.

Allow only features with a documented prediction-time contract.

Interpretation

Feature availability is a semantic property of the deployment workflow, not a property that can be inferred from a column name alone. The same field could be valid in one scoring workflow and invalid in another if the decision moment changes.

Engineering implication

Making the contract explicit creates a reusable interface between modeling, data engineering, and serving systems. Model features can be reviewed against operational availability before a pipeline reaches production rather than after an incident.

Model Results

MEASURED PROJECT-DEFINED METRIC
Empirical comparison

Model quality is reported twice: once under the violating information condition and again under the information set that can actually exist at deployment.

The purpose of this comparison is not to search for the model with the largest possible headline metric. It is to quantify how much apparent performance depends on a forbidden information path and then retain the score produced by the deployment-valid pipeline.

Logistic Regression and Histogram Gradient Boosting are kept as fixed benchmark models. No AutoML or broad model search is used, which keeps the experiment focused on information integrity rather than introducing model-selection effects into the comparison.

Evaluation frame

Two fixed model families are evaluated on the frozen benchmark.

ROC AUC, PR AUC, calibration, ranking yield, and related release metrics are retained.

The deployment-valid result is treated as the trustworthy estimate even when it is lower.

What changes when the model is evaluated with deployment-time information only?

Duration inflates the observed HGB test metrics.

In S1, HGB ROC AUC changes from 0.569 to 0.690 when the current-call duration condition is included.

Evidence to retain
  • Performance is compared under identical release definitions rather than through a new model-search procedure.
  • Ranking and calibration evidence are both retained; ROC AUC is not used as the sole release signal.
  • Project-defined leakage and campaign-yield metrics describe distortion relative to the safe benchmark.

Prefer the lower metric that can exist in production.

Interpretation

A lower deployment-valid metric can be more useful than a higher score produced from an impossible information state. The comparison should therefore be read as a correction of the evaluation boundary, not as evidence that the model suddenly became worse.

Business interpretation

Inflated ranking quality can propagate into campaign-volume, staffing, prioritization, and ROI assumptions. Connecting model metrics to conversions per 1,000 contacts makes that downstream planning risk visible to non-modeling stakeholders.

Audit Evidence

DERIVED CONTROLLED INJECTION
Independent validation

Release evidence is reconciled independently before the dashboard treats it as a publication-ready result.

The validation layer checks that released metric effects can be reproduced from the frozen benchmark outputs and that scenario, model, and reconciliation counts agree with the release package. This separates presentation logic from the calculations that generated the benchmark.

The result is intentionally stronger than a visual inspection of charts: sixty released effects reconcile with zero mismatches, and the controlled duplicate-overlap scenario independently confirms the expected cross-split overlap count.

Validation boundary

Release tables are treated as frozen source evidence.

Dashboard rendering does not silently recompute benchmark business logic.

Internal reconciliation validates consistency; it is not an external replication study.

All 60 released effects reconciled with zero mismatches.

Evidence to retain
  • 60 released metric effects reconcile independently.
  • Reconciliation reports 0 metric-effect mismatches.
  • The controlled duplicate-overlap scenario contains 618 confirmed train/test overlaps.

Treat integrity evidence as a release dependency.

No model result should bypass the feature, split, transformation, duplication, and reconciliation checks.

Interpretation

Reconciliation reduces the risk that a polished dashboard silently diverges from the benchmark that supports it. The same frozen release objects serve the research figures, public claims, and release decision.

Reproducibility implication

This architecture creates a traceable path from benchmark result to visual artifact. Reviewers can distinguish measured evidence, derived metrics, controlled injections, interpretation, and limitations without requiring the presentation layer to recreate the experiment.

Publication

CLAIM REGISTER PUBLIC USE APPROVED
Claim governance

Public communication is treated as a governed output of the benchmark rather than a separate storytelling exercise.

Each publication-facing statement is tied to a claim identifier, evidence class, scope, calculation or evidence source, caveat, and approval status. This prevents an illustrative preview or an unsupported interpretation from quietly becoming a factual benchmark claim in a portfolio page, manuscript, or social post.

Eight claims are approved for public use in the frozen register. Preview-only and unsupported claims remain explicitly unapproved. The dashboard surfaces that boundary so the publication layer can remain persuasive without overstating what the experiment proves.

Publication control

Public statements consume the frozen claim register.

Evidence classes remain visible so measured results are not mixed with interpretation or controlled injections.

Approval applies to the current benchmark scope, not to external generalization.

Which Project 7 claims can safely appear in public artifacts?

Eight claims are approved for public use.

Preview-only claims and unsupported claims remain explicitly unapproved.

Evidence to retain
  • Eight frozen claims are approved for public use.
  • PREVIEW_ONLY claims are not approved as released evidence.
  • UNSUPPORTED claims remain outside the public-use boundary.

Public outputs must consume the frozen claim register.

Do not silently invent new benchmark claims or reinterpret preview-only values as released evidence.

Interpretation

Claim governance is part of technical reproducibility. A benchmark can be computationally correct and still become misleading if the public narrative drops caveats, merges evidence classes, or promotes an exploratory value into a final result.

Recruiter and reviewer value

The publication layer demonstrates more than dashboard creation: it shows a complete analytical control system spanning experimental design, release validation, evidence provenance, interpretation, and responsible public communication.
